Project Modula: Can Music Preferences Improve Numerical Music Ratings?

Collecting expert ratings of generated music is expensive. Pairwise comparisons offer a potentially cheaper alternative: instead of assigning a numerical score, a listener chooses which of two clips they prefer.

Project Modula explores a simple question: Can relatively cheap preference data supplement expensive numerical ratings—and help us predict human scores more accurately?

Our experiments found that a MusicEval-trained evaluator transferred reasonably well to Music Arena preferences. However, learning from those preferences barely improved numerical-score prediction on MusicEval, even when very few human ratings were available.

Two datasets, two kinds of judgment

MusicEval contains 2,748 generated music clips, mostly ten seconds or shorter. Each clip receives five expert ratings, giving 13,740 individual ratings in total. The ratings use a 1–5 scale, allow fractional values, and cover two dimensions: overall musical impression and text–audio alignment.

Our training split contained 1,648 clips and 8,240 individual ratings.

Music Arena collects relative preferences. A listener sees a text prompt, hears two generated tracks, and chooses A, B, a tie, or “both bad.” Unlike MusicEval, it does not provide separate numerical scores for musical quality and text alignment. Based on my own experience rating these tracks, I suspect listeners’ choices reflect a mixture of both.

The Music Arena snapshot we used contained 8,117 comparison records. After excluding ties, “both bad” votes, and records with missing audio, 3,660 decisive comparisons remained. Our downloaded subset comprised 293 training comparisons and 64 validation comparisons, covering 714 audio files and approximately 20.5 hours of music.

The datasets also differ in duration. Music Arena tracks can be much longer than MusicEval clips, and the two tracks in a comparison need not have equal lengths.

A promising transfer result—with a strong baseline

The MusicEval-trained evaluator correctly predicted 248 of 357 Music Arena preferences, or 69.5%.

That initially looked encouraging. But an independent recomputation revealed a surprisingly competitive baseline: always choose the longer clip.

Evaluated comparisons Our evaluator Choose the longer clip
All 357 69.5% 66.9%
Most confident 50% 79.9% 73.2%
Most confident 25% 83.3% 74.4%

On the subsets where the evaluator was most confident, its accuracy increased, and its advantage over the duration baseline widened.

These results suggest some transfer between the datasets. They also show why the baseline matters: duration alone predicts a substantial fraction of listener choices in this sample. The evaluator’s overall accuracy therefore deserves a more cautious interpretation than the headline number suggests.

The hypothesis: use rankings to improve scores

We then asked whether transfer could work in the other direction:

Can Music Arena preferences help an evaluator predict numerical MusicEval ratings more accurately?

We used a two-stage linear Comparison Regression approach, following Singh’s method. The idea is to learn a predictive direction from pairwise comparisons, then use that information when fitting numerical ratings.

Project Modula applies this computational structure across datasets. That introduces a possible failure mode: Music Arena listeners and MusicEval experts may judge music differently. A direction that predicts preference in one dataset may contribute little to numerical scores in the other.

The broad possibility of useful transfer is difficult to rule out with one experiment. The specific hypothesis we tested, however, is falsifiable: does Arena-derived information improve held-out MusicEval score prediction under this linear setup?

Experiment 1: Does more Arena data help?

Increasing the Arena training data from roughly 100 to roughly 200 comparisons stabilized the Arena coefficient and improved pairwise-ranking prediction by about 6%.

Yet this improvement did not translate into a meaningful improvement in the augmented Comparison Regression model’s numerical-score predictions.

The distinction matters. Learning to predict Arena preferences better does not necessarily mean learning information that is useful for MusicEval scores.

Within the range we tested, the results gave us little reason to expect that simply adding more Arena comparisons would solve the transfer problem. They do not establish that larger datasets or different model classes could never help.

Experiment 2: Can rankings help when numerical labels are scarce?

Perhaps the scores-only model already had enough human ratings to learn everything the Arena signal could offer. If so, comparison data might become more useful when numerical labels were scarce.

We tested that possibility using only 10, 25, 50, or 100 human labels.

The table reports mean squared error; lower is better.

Human labels Scores-only Basic CLR Augmented CLR Direction-aware
10 0.681675 0.866996 0.681457 0.680511
25 0.498317 0.751618 0.498164 0.499978
50 0.420333 0.724187 0.420135 0.423539
100 0.367369 0.718005 0.367221 0.368251

The augmented model stayed extremely close to the scores-only baseline. Its numerical improvements were tiny, while basic CLR performed substantially worse. The direction-aware variant showed no consistent advantage.

Even with very few numerical labels, Arena preferences provided little additional predictive value in this setup.

What we learned

The clearest result is that predicting preferences across datasets and improving numerical-score prediction are different achievements.

Our MusicEval evaluator predicted Music Arena choices reasonably well, especially on its most confident comparisons. But the Arena-derived signal added almost nothing to MusicEval score prediction, both with scarce labels and with roughly 8,000 individual training ratings.

This narrows the original hypothesis. The experiments provide little support for adding an Arena-derived linear signal to the existing linear score predictor. They leave open whether transfer could work through a different representation, a nonlinear model, or an approach that explicitly accounts for differences in listeners and judging criteria.

Cheap rankings remain an appealing source of supervision. In this experiment, however, they did not meaningfully substitute for—or add value to—numerical human ratings.

Editorial note: I left out the “84% score-prediction accuracy” claim because the draft does not define that metric. It needs a metric name and evaluation setting before publication.
